Recent work cautions against equating sequential accuracy with meaningful temporal reasoning. [Oh and Cho (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.09722) introduce a recency-bias metric and report improved recommendation performance after mitigating excessive recent-item emphasis. [Liu et al. (RecSys 2025)](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748042) show that random history shuffling mixes user-behavior dependencies with item-availability effects; their constrained shuffling respects each item’s first appearance. [Petrov et al. (2026)](https://research.atspotify.com/2026/10/do-sequential-recommendation-benchmarks-require-higher-order-sequence-modelling) find history-aware pairwise models outperform SASRec/eSASRec reproductions on four of five benchmarks. Thus, useful older-history contributions need not imply higher-order contextualization; results do not directly establish behavior on the four requested categories.

Suggested diagnostic synthesis: compare intact histories against equal-count recent removal, older removal, and repeated seeded shuffles. Preserve the last item in one shuffle condition to separate last-item dependence from earlier-order sensitivity; keep candidate sets and unseen-item eligibility fixed across perturbations. Measure target-score and rank changes, top-10 overlap, validation HR@10 differences, and cosine distance between final sequence representations. Ablate contextual, pooled-history, and recency branches where the architecture exposes them. Small representation and ranking changes suggest weak history dependence; large representation changes with stable rankings suggest changes irrelevant to candidate discrimination. Compare last-item and recency-weighted pooled controls, and test training-objective changes separately. These are proposed model-sensitivity probes, not established measures of causal preferences: deletion changes length and positions, shuffling can create implausible histories, and repeated interactions alone do not establish an underlying interest.
